objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain the symptoms, causes, effects and fixes of every aeromedical condition on the CFI ACS list, apply the alcohol and drug rules, teach ADM, SRM and CRM, and spot each problem in a learner (or in yourself) early enough to fix it before it hurts a lesson or a flight.
why: About 80 percent of aviation accidents are human factors related, and the human factor has not changed with new technology [[25:23|AIH 1-19]]. During flight instruction you are usually the only person who sees a learner under pressure, so you are the one who can tell safe from unsafe actions and notice trouble early [[25:48|AIH 2-15]]. You also carry two pilots' aeromedical risks: yours and the learner's [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

warmup: Think first: your learner shows up for a stall lesson, smiles, and says "I'm good to go." You both know the IMSAFE checklist. Yet the handbooks say a fatigued pilot asked if he is too tired may answer "no," and that a tired learner's mistakes show to others before he feels anything. What could you watch for, and what questions could you ask, that would tell you more than "I'm good to go"? Now turn it around: who checks you?

key_terms.def: Oxygen-rich blood is not flowing to the tissues that need it, for example from high G loads or from cold that cuts circulation to the hands and feet [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Breathing too fast and too deep, which blows off carbon dioxide. A stressful moment can start it without the pilot noticing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].
Closing the mouth, pinching the nose and gently trying to blow through the nostrils to open the Eustachian tube when swallowing or yawning does not clear the ears [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].
An abrupt head movement in a long constant-rate turn creates a false feeling of rotation on a different axis. The AIM calls it the most overwhelming illusion in flight [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].
Dissolved nitrogen comes out of solution as bubbles when pressure drops; the most common symptom is joint pain, the bends [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
Anything that causes stress. The AIH groups stressors as physical, physiological and psychological [[25:28|AIH 1-24]].

Short-term tiredness after strain, monotony or lost sleep. Its signs, such as errors in timing and neglect of secondary tasks, show to others before the pilot feels them [[25:46|AIH 2-13]] [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].
An involuntary sleep lapse of a few seconds to a few minutes that comes as fatigue progresses [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].
Limits more restrictive than the regulations, set from your own experience and proficiency: the difference between legal and smart or safe [[30:13|RMH 2-1]].

Managing all resources on board and outside, before and during flight, so a single pilot gets a safe outcome; it includes ADM, risk, task and automation management, CFIT awareness and situational awareness [[25:19|AIH 1-15]].
Also called learner centered grading: the learner assesses the flight first, then you compare your assessment with theirs in a detailed discussion [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].
Pushing aside information that does not fit what you expect instead of letting it trigger an internal "uh-oh." Not the same as expectation bias [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

chunks.title: Hypoxia and hyperventilation: teach the difference

body.p: Hypoxia means not enough oxygen, and the brain is the main worry because any loss of mental function can lead to a fatal error [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]. Teach the four types by cause: hypoxic (low oxygen pressure at altitude), hypemic (blood cannot carry it, CO is the most common cause), stagnant (blood is not flowing, from G loads or cold) and histotoxic (cells cannot use it, from alcohol and drugs) [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]] [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

The AIM gives the numbers a learner should remember. Night vision starts to suffer at a cabin altitude as low as 5,000 ft, other big effects usually wait until 12,000 ft, and performance can seriously deteriorate within 15 minutes at 15,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. For best protection it recommends oxygen above 10,000 ft by day and above 5,000 ft at night; the rule makes required crew use it after 30 minutes above 12,500 ft up to 14,000 ft, and at all times above 14,000 ft [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]] [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

Hypoxia is hard to recognize when it comes on slowly. The AIM says a person's symptoms do not vary, so experiencing them once in an altitude chamber makes them much easier to spot later [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. The worst symptom to teach is the false sense of security: the pilot believes everything is normal [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Treatment is lower altitude, supplemental oxygen, or both [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

Hyperventilation happens more often among pilots than is generally recognized. It seldom fully incapacitates, but its symptoms alarm an uninformed pilot, and the anxiety makes the breathing worse [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]. Symptoms: visual impairment, lightheadedness, tingling, hot and cold sensations, muscle spasms and finally unconsciousness [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]]. The fix is to slow the breathing; talking aloud or breathing into a paper bag helps, and recovery is usually rapid [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

callout.text: Instructor angle: an anxious learner on a first stall or steep turn lesson is a hyperventilation candidate. Ask them to talk you through what they are doing. Talking aloud slows the breathing, and the learner-tells step of telling-and-doing gives you a reason to ask [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
The early symptoms of the two overlap, and both can happen at once. If you are on oxygen, set the regulator to 100 percent and check the system first, then work on breathing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

check.q: Why does the AIM say chamber training helps a pilot recognize hypoxia later?
check.a: Because a given person's hypoxia symptoms do not vary, so experiencing them once teaches you your own warning signs [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

chunks.title: Middle ear, sinuses and scuba nitrogen

body.p: Middle ear and sinus problems come from trapped gas. Climbing, middle ear air usually escapes down the Eustachian tube by itself; descending, the pilot must open the tube by swallowing, yawning, tensing the throat or the Valsalva maneuver [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. A cold, sore throat or nasal allergy can block it: an ear block brings severe pain and hearing loss for hours to days and can rupture the eardrum [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. A sinus block happens most often in descent, with pain above the eyebrows or in the upper cheeks, aching upper teeth or bloody mucus [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

Prevention is not flying with an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergy. Decongestant sprays and drops usually do not give adequate protection, oral decongestants have side effects that can impair performance, and a block that does not clear soon after landing needs a physician [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]] [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]. In flight, slow descent rates can reduce the pain of a sinus block [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

callout.text: Instructor angle: illness slows learning because it dulls vision, hearing and feeling [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. A learner with a cold who wants to fly the pattern for an hour is asking for many descents. Make it a ground lesson.

body.p: Dissolved nitrogen in the bloodstream after scuba dives is the other gas problem. Diving loads the body with extra nitrogen; flying too soon lets it come out as bubbles at low cabin pressure and can create a serious in-flight emergency [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]. The waits: at least 12 hours before flying up to 8,000 ft after a dive with no decompression stops, at least 24 hours after a dive that needed decompression stops, and at least 24 hours after any dive before flying above 8,000 ft. These are actual MSL altitudes, not cabin altitudes [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

DCS shows up in different places: the bends in large joints, neurologic signs such as confusion, headache and vision changes, the chokes in the lungs, and skin bends with itching and mottled skin [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]]. If it happens: 100 percent oxygen, emergency descent, land as soon as possible, keep a painful joint still and get medical help even if symptoms fade. Symptoms can also start after landing [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

callout.text: 12, 24, 24: twelve hours for an easy dive up to 8,000 ft, twenty-four for a decompression dive, twenty-four for any dive above 8,000 ft [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

check.q: A learner back from a dive trip asks if a nose spray will let her fly with a stuffy nose. What does the AIM say?
check.a: Do not fly with an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergy; decongestant sprays usually do not give adequate protection [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

chunks.title: Spatial disorientation: explain it, then demonstrate it safely

body.p: Spatial disorientation is not knowing the airplane's position, attitude or movement in space. The brain uses three systems: vestibular (inner ear), somatosensory (skin, muscles, joints) and visual. In VMC the eyes usually win; take them away and false sensations can disorient a pilot quickly [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

The key teaching point is the semicircular canal threshold. A rotation of 2 degrees per second or less is not detected, and in a steady turn the fluid catches up with the canal so the feeling of turning fades. Stopping the turn then feels like a turn the other way [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. That one idea explains the leans and the graveyard spiral.
The PHAK gives instructors a set of in-flight demonstrations, flown by the instructor while the learner sits with eyes closed or head down [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]]:

bullets: Climbing while accelerating: straight and level, then accelerate; the usual illusion is a climb [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].
Climbing while turning: a slow, coordinated turn of about 1.5 G (about 50 degrees of bank) for 90 degrees feels like a climb [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].
Diving while turning: the same turn, eyes kept closed until the recovery is about half done [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].
Tilting to right or left: a slight skid to the left, wings level, feels like a tilt to the right [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].
Reversal of motion: a smooth roll to about 45 degrees while holding heading and pitch gives a strong sense of rotation the other way [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].
Diving or rolling beyond the vertical plane: a head movement timed with a roll toward 30 to 40 degrees can produce intense disorientation [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

body.p: The objectives are to show how susceptible the body is, that attitude judged by feel is often false, how head movement makes it worse, and to build confidence in the instruments. Even feeling nothing is a good demonstration, because it proves bank and roll cannot be detected [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]] [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

callout.text: Never do these maneuvers at low altitude or without an instructor or safety pilot [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]]. Brief who has the controls first: the AIH's positive three-step exchange of flight controls belongs in every preflight briefing [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

body.p: Defenses to teach: get instrument training before flying in visibility under 3 miles or with no visible horizon, avoid sudden head movement in takeoffs, turns and approaches, be rested and healthy because illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue, sleep loss and mild hypoxia all raise susceptibility, and above all trust the instruments [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]] [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

check.q: During the climbing-while-turning demo your learner says she felt nothing. Was the demo wasted?
check.a: No. Feeling nothing still demonstrates that bank and roll cannot be detected by the body [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].

chunks.title: Optical illusions on approach: teach the pattern

body.p: Optical illusions are mostly a landing problem: surface features and the atmosphere make the pilot misjudge height above and distance from the threshold [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Illusions rank among the most common factors cited in fatal accidents [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

Give learners one rule and let them sort the cases: whatever makes you feel high makes you fly low, and whatever makes you feel low or close makes you fly high. A narrower runway, an upsloping runway, featureless terrain, rain on the windscreen and haze all lead to a lower approach; a wider runway and bright runway lights with dark surroundings lead to a higher one; flying into fog feels like pitching up, so pilots steepen the approach [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]] [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]. Overflying terrain with few lights for height cues can also produce a lower than normal approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

bullets: Anticipate illusions at unfamiliar airports, especially at night or in bad weather; check the airport diagram and Chart Supplement for slope, terrain and lighting [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]] [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Cross-check the altimeter on every approach, day and night [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Look the airport over from the air before landing when you can [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Use VASI, PAPI or an electronic glideslope, and the visual descent point on nonprecision charts [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Know that approach accidents become more likely when an emergency or other activity distracts from usual procedures [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

callout.text: Application: when your training airport has a single runway, the first landing at a narrower or sloped field is the lesson. Brief the expected illusion on the ground, then let the learner fly it and compare the PAPI with the picture out the window.

check.q: At night over dark farmland with few lights, your learner's approach is lower than normal. What does the AIM say is happening?
check.a: Overflying terrain with few lights for height cues can cause a lower than normal approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

chunks.title: Motion sickness and carbon monoxide in the training airplane

body.p: Motion sickness comes from the brain getting conflicting messages about the body. Symptoms: general discomfort, nausea, dizziness, paleness, sweating and vomiting. It often appears on early flights and usually goes away within the first few lessons, and anxiety and stress feed it [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Tell learners it is no reflection on their ability as pilots [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

bullets: End the instructional flight as soon as early airsickness appears. Resistance usually builds fast, and flights can then be lengthened step by step [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].
Keep the learner busy: learners are much less apt to get sick while flying the controls themselves [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].
Fresh air on the face helps; rough air, abrupt maneuvers, tension and apprehension make it worse [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].
Medicines like Dramamine can help passengers but are not recommended for the pilot because they cause drowsiness [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

body.p: Carbon monoxide poisoning is the hidden one. CO is colorless, odorless and tasteless, and most light airplane heaters warm air over the exhaust manifold, so a crack or leaking seal can feed it into the cabin [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]]. It bonds to hemoglobin about 200 times more easily than oxygen, causing hypemic hypoxia, and the body needs up to 48 hours to get rid of it [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Symptoms: headache, blurred vision, dizziness, drowsiness and loss of muscle power [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

callout.text: Smell exhaust, or feel those symptoms with the heater on: heater off, fresh air vents and windows open, oxygen if available, and get medical help if symptoms are severe or continue after landing [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]] [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]]. You breathe the same air as the learner, so your own judgment is going too. CO can be dangerous with no exhaust smell at all; a cheap detector helps [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

check.q: Your learner turns pale and sweaty during steep turns. What does the AIH say to do with the lesson?
check.a: Terminate the instructional flight as soon as early sickness appears, then build flight length up as the learner develops resistance [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

chunks.title: Stress: reading it in your learner

body.p: Stress is the body's response to demands. It releases hormones such as adrenaline and raises blood sugar, heart rate, breathing, blood pressure and sweating [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Acute stress is an immediate threat; chronic stress is a load that exceeds a person's ability to cope, and a pilot in that state is not safe to exercise airman privileges and should see a physician [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

Some stress keeps a person alert. Performance rises with stress, peaks, then falls off fast once stress exceeds the ability to cope [[25:27|AIH 1-23]]. Note for learners: the regulations list medical conditions that require grounding, and stress is not among them, so only an honest self-assessment catches it [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]. Most pilots do not leave stress on the ground; when difficulties are greater than usual, delay the flight [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

bullets: If a learner seems distracted or struggles with the lesson, ask: were you uncomfortable or tired? Is something else in your life pulling at you [[25:28|AIH 1-24]]?

A learner who keeps canceling in good weather may be dreading the lesson content, such as stalls, landings or the first solo. Explain the maneuver in more detail and encourage them [[25:28|AIH 1-24]].
Treat fears as normal, and before stalls describe the aerodynamics, the sensations to expect and the recovery [[25:45|AIH 2-12]].
Coping techniques to suggest: relaxation time, physical fitness, better time management and realistic goals [[25:28|AIH 1-24]].

callout.text: Abnormal reactions to stress: extreme over-cooperation, painstaking self-control, inappropriate laughter or singing, very rapid mood changes, excellent morale followed by deep depression, or severe anger at the instructor or others. None is proof, but any of them under stress calls for careful evaluation [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

check.q: Name the three stressor types in AIH Figure 1-13 with one example each.
check.a: Physical (noise, vibration, temperature extremes), physiological (fatigue, missed meals, illness) and psychological (a death in the family, mental workload) [[25:28|AIH 1-24]].

body.p: Fatigue is one of the most treacherous hazards because it may not be apparent until serious errors are made. Acute fatigue is the normal tiredness after strain, immobility, heavy mental workload, emotional pressure, monotony or lost sleep; chronic fatigue comes when there is not enough recovery between episodes and needs a prolonged rest [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]. The only effective treatment is adequate sleep [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

As fatigue progresses it causes more errors of omission, then errors of commission, then microsleeps. Sleep-deprived pilots may feel fine during preflight and departure; the sleepiness comes once they are established on altitude and heading [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]. Skill fatigue shows as timing disruption and a narrowed perceptual field that neglects the periphery [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

head: Sign of acute fatigue you can see
What it looks like in a lesson (application)
rows: Inattention and distractibility [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Missed radio calls, staring at one gauge
Errors in timing [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Flare late, rollout of turns late
Neglect of secondary tasks [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Checklist items skipped, trim forgotten
Loss of accuracy and control [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Altitude and airspeed wander more than earlier in the lesson
Lack of awareness of error accumulation [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Learner says the lesson is going well
Irritability [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Snaps at you or ATC

body.p: These signs show to others before the learner notices any physical sign [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. Fatigue is the primary consideration in setting the length and frequency of lessons: continue only while the learner is alert and receptive, and give a break when fatigue appears [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

callout.text: Your own limit: in any 24 consecutive hours a flight instructor may not conduct more than 8 hours of flight training [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]]. Eight hours is a ceiling, not a target; monitor your own IMSAFE all day [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: Why can't you rely on a tired learner telling you they are tired?
check.a: The deficiencies of acute fatigue are apparent to others before the individual notices any physical sign, and a goal-oriented pilot tends to deny personal limits [[25:46|AIH 2-13]] [[25:13|AIH 1-9]].

body.p: Dehydration and nutrition: dehydration is a critical loss of body water from hot flight decks and ramps, wind, humidity and diuretics such as coffee, tea, alcohol and caffeinated soft drinks [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]]. It reduces alertness and slows decisions, and the first effect is fatigue, then dizziness, weakness, nausea, tingling hands and feet, cramps and extreme thirst [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Long flights in summer heat or at high altitude raise the risk, because dry air at altitude speeds water loss [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

bullets: Daily guide: two to four quarts of water every 24 hours [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
Thirst starts late, at about a 1.5 quart deficit or 2 percent of body weight, and a sip turns it off [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
In flight: about one quart per hour in severe heat stress, one pint per hour in moderate heat, whether thirsty or not [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
Heatstroke may show as dehydration or only as a sudden collapse; carry water, wear light porous clothing and a hat under a canopy, and ventilate the flight deck [[25:47|AIH 2-14]].

body.p: Nutrition: eat regular balanced meals and bring a snack for you and your passengers [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. Missed meals lead to low blood sugar, a physiological stressor [[25:28|AIH 1-24]], and the AIH fatigue countermeasures include high-protein meals and plenty of fluids [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]. Some publications use the E in IMSAFE for Eating to make the same point [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

Hypothermia: the FAA handbooks used here do not define hypothermia or list its symptoms and treatment. What they do say about cold: it reduces blood flow to the hands and feet (stagnant hypoxia) [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], extreme cold raises the body's oxygen demand and so its susceptibility to hypoxia [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]], temperature extremes are a physical stressor [[25:28|AIH 1-24]], and a learner distracted by extremes of temperature cannot learn at a normal rate [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. For trips over remote areas, the PAVE check asks whether proper clothing, water and survival gear are on board [[25:10|AIH 1-6]].

callout.text: Application: on a winter cross-country, have the learner dress for a forced landing, not for the heated cabin, and get hypothermia signs and first aid from a medical source or an AME. Say on the checkride that the FAA handbooks are silent on it, then give what they do say about cold.

check.q: Why can't a pilot rely on thirst to stay hydrated?
check.a: Thirst starts only at about a 1.5 quart deficit, or 2 percent of body weight, and a small sip turns it off, so replacing the water is delayed [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

chunks.title: The alcohol and drug rules, taught as three limits

body.p: 14 CFR 91.17(a) bars anyone from acting or attempting to act as a crewmember within 8 hours after drinking any alcohol, while under the influence of alcohol, while using any drug that affects their faculties contrary to safety, or with an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater in blood or breath [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].

The RMH gives you a clean way to teach it: a time limit (8 hours), a quantity limit (below 0.04) and a performance limit (no flight duty while under the influence). Aftereffects such as dehydration, hangover and headache can stay a hazard well past 8 hours [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]. Learners often remember only the 8 hours, so make them say all three.

head: Rule
What it says
rows: Except in an emergency, no pilot may allow a person who appears intoxicated or under the influence of drugs to be carried, except a medical patient under proper care [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]

Submit to an alcohol test when an authorized law enforcement officer asks; when the FAA has a reasonable basis to believe (a)(1), (a)(2) or (a)(4) was violated, release on request the results of alcohol tests taken within 4 hours after acting as a crewmember [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]
The same 4-hour test-result release applies to drug tests when the FAA has reason to believe 91.17(a)(3) was violated [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]

No PIC or required pilot crewmember duty while you know or have reason to know of a condition, or take medication or treatment, that would make you fail the medical standard you need [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53]]

body.p: The regulations have no specific list of medications; the two that matter are 61.53 and the drug clause of 91.17 [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. The FAA states that marijuana is an illicit drug under federal law and its use by airmen is prohibited, whatever state law allows [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

callout.text: Your medical as a CFI: you need at least a third-class medical when exercising flight instructor privileges as PIC or as a required flightcrew member, unless operating under BasicMed (61.113(i)) [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23]]. Tell student pilots to see an AME early so they do not pay for training they cannot finish [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

check.q: Name the three limits the RMH uses to describe the alcohol rule.
check.a: A time limit (no drinking within 8 hours), a quantity limit (below 0.04) and a performance limit (no flight duty while under the influence) [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

chunks.title: Effects of alcohol, drugs and over-the-counter medicine

body.p: Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that acts much like a general anesthetic. Even small amounts impair judgment, coordination, vision, memory and attention, and one drink can affect vision and hearing [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]]. It produces histotoxic hypoxia: one ounce can equal about 2,000 ft of extra physiological altitude [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], and altitude multiplies its effects so two drinks may act like three or four [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

bullets: About 3 hours to clear one mixed drink or one beer; large amounts can remain over 16 hours; a hangover is still being under the influence [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
Nothing speeds up the destruction of alcohol; the AIM's rule is 12 to 24 hours from bottle to throttle [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].
Alcohol can cause inner-ear disturbance and spatial disorientation for up to 48 hours [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

body.p: Drugs: some, such as tranquilizers, sedatives, strong pain relievers and cough suppressants, impair judgment, memory, alertness, coordination, vision and calculation directly; antihistamines, blood pressure drugs, muscle relaxants and anti-diarrhea and motion sickness agents can do it as side effects. Any nervous system depressant makes a pilot more susceptible to hypoxia [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

Over-the-counter medications are where learners get caught. Antihistamines and decongestants can cause drowsiness and cognitive deficits; diphenhydramine has a long half-life, so its side effects last [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. Drugs with no side effects on the ground can cause problems at fairly low altitudes, and fatigue, stress, dehydration and poor nutrition raise susceptibility even to a drug tolerated before [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. Herbal and dietary supplements and energy boosters can have side effects too [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

head: OTC item
Flight effect to teach
rows: Caffeine
Impaired judgment, sleep disturbance, dehydration through urine output [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]]
Antacid
Carbon dioxide released at altitude; distension can cause abdominal pain and mask other problems [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]]
Aspirin
Two aspirin can contribute to hypoxia and hyperventilation [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]]
Aspirin, acetaminophen, ibuprofen at the correct dose
Few side effects; flying usually not restricted [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]

callout.text: New medicine: wait 48 hours after the first dose. Sedating or dizzying medicine: wait five maximal dosing intervals after the last dose. Never mix drugs with alcohol [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

Application: ask the learner "What did you take today?" rather than "Are you OK?" The illness behind the medicine can be disqualifying by itself [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]], and when in doubt the answer is to ask an AME before flying [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

check.q: Why might an antacid matter at altitude?
check.a: It can release carbon dioxide at altitude, and the distension may cause acute abdominal pain and mask other medical problems [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

chunks.title: Teaching ADM with SRM, and CRM where there is a crew

body.p: ADM is a systematic way to find the best course of action for a set of circumstances. Teach it as a system with risk management, situational awareness and SRM, woven through the whole course rather than as a separate subject [[25:23|AIH 1-19]] [[25:24|AIH 1-20]]. The poor judgment chain is the best way to show learners why: breaking one link is usually enough to change the outcome [[25:23|AIH 1-19]].

SRM is how a single pilot does it, and using ATC and Flight Service repeats the principles of CRM [[25:19|AIH 1-15]]. The 5P check reviews the Plan, Plane, Pilot, Passengers and Programming at preflight, before takeoff, at the midpoint (hourly on flights over 2 hours), before descent and before the final approach fix or pattern entry [[25:20|AIH 1-16]] [[25:21|AIH 1-17]]. Late night, fatigue and sustained flight above 5,000 ft can make a pilot less critical and more compliant just as the hardest part of the flight arrives [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].

CRM is the crew version: the effective use of all resources, people, hardware and information, to make good decisions [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]]. You will meet professional crew pilots who know CRM and threat and error management but are not used to flying alone without their employer's support; adapt their training to single-pilot risk management [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

head: System safety phase
What you teach
rows: I. Stick and rudder
Build confidence in flying the airplane first [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]
II. Add the hazards
Discuss runway, obstacles, weight and density altitude on the ground, at no extra flight time [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]
III. Complex scenario
Script several safety issues into one realistic flight, then act as mentor [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]

body.p: A good scenario is not a test, has no single correct answer and no obvious answer, engages all three learning domains, is interactive, does not promote errors, promotes situational awareness and decisions, and requires time-pressured decisions [[25:31|AIH 1-27]]. Let learners make real decisions about fitness to fly, weather and equipment, and have them assess the weather and make a go/no-go call before each flight, even though the final choice stays with you [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

bullets: Explain: the learner can identify and describe the risks but needs prompting [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].
Practice: the learner applies SRM; your coaching quickly corrects minor errors [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].
Manage/Decide: the learner gathers the data, weighs options and decides with no instructor intervention needed [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].
Not Observed: the event did not happen or was not required [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

callout.text: Numerical FRATs need care: a low score can hide one extreme risk, such as a line of embedded thunderstorms, that the list never captured [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

check.q: At which SRM grade is instructor intervention not required for the safe completion of the flight?

chunks.title: Hazardous attitudes, distractions and bias: spot them in a learner

body.p: Hazardous attitudes: recognize the thought, label it as hazardous, then say the antidote; antidotes should be memorized so they come to mind on their own [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. As an instructor you should be able to spot them in a learner, because recognition is the first step to neutralizing them [[25:26|AIH 1-22]].

Teach it with stories like Steve's in Figure 1-12: learners can be asked to identify the attitude and its antidote in a flight scenario [[25:27|AIH 1-23]]. Watch the quick learner too: a learner who finds training easy may develop a hazardous attitude about their ability, so point out the potential and teach the antidote. Hazardous attitudes need to be noticed immediately and corrected [[25:27|AIH 1-23]].

Distractions and task prioritization: many accidents start with a minor problem, such as a gauge reading wrong, that pulls attention away from controlling the airplane [[25:17|AIH 1-13]]. In a go-around, power, airspeed and configuration come first; telling the tower comes after. In an emergency the first priority is to fly the airplane [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

Loss of situational awareness: as workload rises the pilot first works faster, then focuses on one item, then becomes task saturated and decides on incomplete information [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]. Raise the workload gradually in a lesson, make sure the learner can recognize overload, and teach the fix: stop, think, slow down and prioritize, and hand tasks to a passenger, the autopilot or ATC [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]. To check awareness, ask about traffic positions, engine indications and position on the chart, or create an imaginary radio problem and see whether the learner stops flying the airplane [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]. Disorientation, both spatial and positional, is the end of that road: getting behind the airplane can lead to not knowing where you are [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]].

Confirmation and expectation bias: expectation bias is a wrong picture that persists despite evidence, such as a pilot who read a changed runway closure NOTAM and still saw the old one. Confirmation bias is suppressing information that does not fit the expectation. Either way the pilot keeps a plan the facts do not support, and fatigue makes both more likely [[30:45|RMH 6-2]] [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Expectation bias is common while taxiing, when a pilot hears the usual clearance instead of the one given [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

callout.text: Defenses to teach: agree on the plan, ask for clarification and question any inconsistency; on the ground you can always stop the airplane; once airborne, slow down or ask ATC for more time [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. Be especially alert to complacency in experienced pilots, such as a flight review in a familiar airplane [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

check.q: How can you test a learner's situational awareness in flight without a real problem?
check.a: Ask about traffic positions, engine indications and position on the chart, or focus them on an imaginary radio problem and see if they stop controlling the airplane or scanning [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

chunks.title: S1 and S2: symptoms to fixes, and an honest self-assessment

body.p: For S1 the examiner wants you to demonstrate and explain at least three K1 conditions, linking symptoms and effects to causes and corrective actions (ACS AI.II.A.S1). Practice a one-line chain for all twelve, for example: tingling, lightheaded, fast breathing in a tense moment; cause, blowing off CO2; fix, slow the breathing and talk aloud [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]] [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

For S2 you assess yourself, including fitness for flight and personal minimums, for the real flight or the examiner's scenario (ACS AI.II.A.S2). Start with IMSAFE [[25:12|AIH 1-8]], then compare the day with your written minimums. The AIH's point is the difference between legal and smart or safe [[25:9|AIH 1-5]].

head: RMH step
What to do
rows: 1. Review weather categories
Know the ceiling and visibility of VFR, MVFR, IFR and LIFR [[30:13|RMH 2-1]]
2. Assess experience and comfort
Fill in your certification, training and experience summary [[30:13|RMH 2-1]]
3. Consider other conditions
Wind, turbulence and performance factors such as shortest runway [[30:15|RMH 2-3]] [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]
4. Assemble and evaluate
Combine into a baseline table [[30:16|RMH 2-4]]
5. Adjust for specific conditions

Figure 2-9 is only a starting point. When several factors apply, adjust once for each: the RMH's worked example (night cross-country to an unfamiliar airport after a full workday) adds 1,000 ft ceiling, 1 mile visibility and 1,000 ft runway. The figure lists at least 500 ft ceiling, 1/2 mile visibility, 500 ft runway and 5 knots less wind [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]
6. Stick to the plan
Written minimums make the no-go call easier to explain [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]

callout.text: Teach the cautions: never adjust minimums to complete a specific flight, change only one variable at a time, and get training and talk to an instructor before a significant change [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

body.p: Model it. Monitor your own aeromedical state with IMSAFE, and build enough trust that learners tell you about their own issues well before the lesson so it can be rescheduled [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. If the day does not support the lesson, say so out loud and change it: stay in the pattern, move to a simulator or ground school, or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

check.q: A learner wants to lower his visibility minimum and his crosswind minimum together for tomorrow's trip. What two RMH cautions apply?
check.a: Do not adjust minimums to complete a specific flight, and adjust only one variable at a time, after training and a talk with an instructor [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Flying a tired learner
Inattention, timing errors, skipped secondary tasks, irritability [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]
Give a break or end the lesson; plan lesson length around fatigue [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Pressing on with airsickness
Paleness, sweating, nausea [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]
End the flight early, fresh air, let them fly; lengthen flights later [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]
Missing hyperventilation
Fast breathing, tingling, lightheaded learner in a tense maneuver [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]]
Slow the breathing, have them talk aloud [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]]
Flying with a cold
Stuffy nose, plans many descents
Ground lesson; sprays usually do not protect [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]
Trusting the learner's "I'm fine"
Goal-oriented learner denies limits [[25:13|AIH 1-9]]
Ask specific IMSAFE questions; ask what they took today [[25:12|AIH 1-8]]
Letting a fixation run
Learner stares at one radio while altitude drifts [[25:17|AIH 1-13]]
Fly the airplane first; stop, think, slow down, prioritize [[25:30|AIH 1-26]]
Ignoring a hazardous attitude
Bragging, rule-bending, "it won't happen to me" [[25:27|AIH 1-23]]
Name it right away and teach the antidote [[25:27|AIH 1-23]]
Accepting the expected clearance
Taxi route or runway flown as usual, not as given [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]
Ask for clarification and question any inconsistency; stop on the ground if unsure [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]
Disorientation demo gone wrong
Low altitude, or unclear who has the controls
Demo only with altitude and a positive exchange of controls [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]] [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]

callout.text: The instructor is a hazard too. Your qualifications, currency, familiarity with the airplane and aeromedical state all belong in the P of PAVE before every lesson [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

check.q: Name two ways the AIH says to reduce workload when a learner becomes overloaded.
check.a: Delegate an item such as finding something on the chart or setting a frequency to a passenger or another pilot, use the autopilot, or ask ATC for help, after stopping, thinking, slowing down and prioritizing [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

f1.caption: Figure 1-12. Learners in training can be asked to identify hazardous attitudes and the corresponding antidotes when presented with flight scenarios. (AIH 1-23)
f1.alt: A two-column table following one pilot, Steve. Macho: he brags and decides to buzz friends at a park; antidote, taking chances is foolish. Anti-authority: he thinks the low-flying rules are too restrictive; antidote, follow the rules, they are usually right. Invulnerability: he has flown this low many times; antidote, it could happen to me. Impulsivity: he yanks back on the yoke near a power line; antidote, not so fast, think first. Resignation: after minor wing damage he thinks effort does not matter; antidote, I'm not helpless, I can make a difference.

f2.caption: Figure 1-7. Countermeasures for coping with fatigue. (AIH 1-14)
f2.alt: A list with pictures of a bed, a glass of water, a steak, a bicycle and a thermometer: long naps of 3 to 4 hours restore alertness for 12 to 15 hours; power naps of 10 to 30 minutes restore it for 3 to 4 hours; eat high-protein meals; drink plenty of fluids; rotate tasks and talk with crew or passengers; keep the flight deck cool; move, stretch and walk around if possible. A note says to allow 15 to 20 minutes after waking before crew duties.

f3.caption: Figure 1-13. Three types of stressors that can affect pilot performance. (AIH 1-24)
f3.alt: Three boxes. Physical stress: environmental conditions such as temperature and humidity extremes, noise, vibration and lack of oxygen. Physiological stress: fatigue, lack of fitness, sleep loss, missed meals and illness. Psychological stress: social or emotional factors such as a death in the family, divorce, a sick child or a demotion, and mental workload.

f4.caption: Figure 17-4. Human sensation of angular acceleration. Stage names are cropped off for the labeling game. (PHAK 17-7)
f4.alt: Four drawings of a semicircular canal with its cupola and endolymph fluid, left to right. In the first and third the hairs stand straight with no fluid flow marked. In the second, fluid arrows deflect the hairs one way. In the fourth, fluid arrows deflect the hairs the opposite way.

f5.caption: Figure 17-10. Signs and symptoms of altitude decompression sickness. (PHAK 17-19)
f5.alt: A table of DCS types. Bends: deep joint pain in elbows, shoulders, hips, wrists, knees and ankles, worse with motion. Neurologic: confusion, headache, vision spots or tunnel vision, extreme fatigue, seizures; spinal cord and peripheral nerve signs such as tingling, weakness and paralysis. Chokes: burning chest pain, shortness of breath, dry cough. Skin bends: itching, crawling sensation, mottled skin and swelling.

f6.caption: Figure 17-7. Runway illusions. (PHAK 17-11)
f6.alt: Paired scenes. A narrower runway makes the pilot fly a lower approach than the dotted normal path; a wider runway makes the pilot fly higher. A downsloping runway leads to a higher approach and an upsloping runway to a lower approach. Text boxes explain each illusion.

f7.caption: Figure 1-14. Accidents often occur when flying task requirements exceed pilot capabilities. The difference between these two factors is called the margin of safety. (AIH 1-26)
f7.alt: A 3D ribbon chart over time from preflight through takeoff, cruise and approach and landing. A pilot capabilities band and a wavy task requirements band run side by side over time; the gap between them is labeled margin of safety. Near approach and landing the task requirements band climbs until it almost meets pilot capabilities.

scenario.title: The Saturday stall lesson
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. Your pre-solo learner, Sam, is booked at 0800 for stalls and steep turns in the practice area at 5,500 ft MSL. He drove home last night from a dive trip; his last dive, with no decompression stops, ended at 1600 yesterday. He has a stuffy nose and took a diphenhydramine allergy tablet at 0600. When you ask how he feels he grins: "I'll be fine, I always am." You gave 6 hours of flight training yesterday, slept about 5 hours, and have three more lessons booked today.

questions.q: Is the dive a problem for a 5,500 ft lesson?
questions.a: Not by itself. Sixteen hours have passed since a no-decompression dive, and the AIM recommends at least 12 hours before flying up to 8,000 ft MSL; above 8,000 ft he would need 24 hours [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]. Keep the lesson below 8,000 ft if you fly at all.

questions.q: What about the stuffy nose on a stall lesson?
questions.a: Stalls mean repeated climbs and descents, and an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergy can cause an ear or sinus block, most often in descent. The AIM's prevention is not flying with that condition; sprays usually do not protect [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]] [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

questions.q: Why does the allergy tablet matter?
questions.a: Diphenhydramine causes drowsiness and has a long half-life [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]], antihistamines make a pilot more susceptible to hypoxia [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]], and 91.17 bars crew duty while using a drug that affects faculties contrary to safety [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]. The PHAK's rule is five maximal dosing intervals after a sedating medicine [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

questions.q: Which hazardous attitude did Sam just show, and what do you do with it?
questions.a: Invulnerability, "it won't happen to me"; the antidote is "it could happen to me" [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. Point it out right away and teach the antidote [[25:27|AIH 1-23]], then let Sam make the go/no-go call himself and discuss it [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

Run IMSAFE on yourself: 5 hours of sleep is a fatigue flag, and acute fatigue calls for staying on the ground [[25:191|AIH 10-7]] [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. Also count your hours: no more than 8 hours of flight training in any 24 consecutive hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]].

questions.q: How do you save the morning?
questions.a: Change the lesson: ground school on aeromedical factors or a simulator session, or reschedule [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]. Use it to set the expectation that Sam tells you about illness and medicine well before a lesson so it can be moved [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

skills.do: The examiner will have you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to "Associate the symptoms and effects for at least three of the conditions listed in K1a through K1l with the cause(s) and corrective action(s)" (ACS AI.II.A.S1). Expect to be handed symptoms (for example tingling and lightheadedness in a tense moment, or a headache with the heater on) and to name the condition, its cause and the fix, then say how you would teach it and spot it in a learner.
skills.practice: Make a 12-row card: condition, symptoms, cause, corrective action, how you would spot it in a learner. Fill it only from PHAK 17-3 to 17-19 [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]] [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]] and AIM 8-1-1 to 8-1-5 [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]] [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]], and for hypothermia write what the sources say about cold. Have a friend read random symptoms aloud while you answer.

skills.do: The examiner will have you demonstrate and simultaneously explain how to "Perform self-assessment, including fitness for flight and personal minimums, for actual flight or a scenario given by the evaluator" (ACS AI.II.A.S2). Expect to run IMSAFE out loud on yourself, compare the day with your written personal minimums and the RMH adjustments, and make and defend a go, no-go or change-the-lesson decision.
skills.practice: Build your own baseline personal minimums with the RMH six steps [[30:13|RMH 2-1]] [[30:17|RMH 2-5]], write them on a card, and before each flight this month say IMSAFE out loud [[25:12|AIH 1-8]] and apply one adjustment for every factor that applies [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

quiz.q: What does the PHAK say about how often hyperventilation happens to pilots?
options: It happens only above 12,500 ft
It happens more often than is generally recognized
It happens only to pilots using supplemental oxygen
It almost always causes full incapacitation
quiz.why: It occurs more often among pilots than is generally recognized and seldom incapacitates completely [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

quiz.q: Your learner breathes fast, feels tingling and is lightheaded on a first stall lesson at 3,500 ft. Besides slowing the breathing, what does the PHAK say helps?
options: Talking aloud
Climbing higher
Turning on the cabin heater
Taking an antihistamine
quiz.why: Slowing the breathing rate, breathing into a paper bag or talking aloud helps overcome hyperventilation [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

quiz.q: In the PHAK's reversal of motion demonstration, what does the learner usually feel?
options: A gentle climb, the same sensation as in the acceleration demo
A slight tilt to the right, with no sense of rolling at all
Falling downward into the roll, toward the lower wing
A strong sense of rotation in the opposite direction
quiz.why: A smooth roll to about 45 degrees while holding heading and pitch creates a strong sense of rotation the other way [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

quiz.q: Which is on the PHAK's list for preventing landing errors from optical illusions?
options: Look at the runway lights continuously and ignore the altimeter
Fly the approach faster than normal to keep a margin over the stall
Stop using the altimeter below 1,000 ft and fly the window picture
Use the visual descent point on nonprecision approach charts
quiz.why: The list includes using the VDP found on many nonprecision approach charts [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

quiz.q: Climbing through 9,000 ft, a passenger who went scuba diving reports joint pain that keeps getting worse. What does the PHAK say to do?
options: Have the passenger move the joint around to work the pain out, then continue
Oxygen at 100 percent, an emergency descent, and land as soon as possible
Level off at 8,000 ft and continue, since DCS clears up below that altitude
Descend, and skip the medical check if the pain is gone by the time you land
quiz.why: For altitude-induced DCS the PHAK says: oxygen mask on with the regulator at 100 percent, begin an emergency descent and land as soon as possible. Keep a painful joint still, and seek medical evaluation even if the symptoms disappear during the descent [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the AIH's listed signs of acute fatigue?
options: Euphoria
Neglect of secondary tasks
Errors in timing
Irritability
quiz.why: The list is inattention, distractibility, errors in timing, neglect of secondary tasks, loss of accuracy and control, lack of awareness of error accumulation, and irritability [[25:47|AIH 2-14]]. Euphoria is a hypoxia symptom [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

quiz.q: According to the AIH, what is the only effective treatment for fatigue?
options: Caffeine
A high-protein meal
Cooler flight deck temperature
Adequate sleep
quiz.why: The only effective treatment for fatigue is adequate sleep [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

quiz.q: PHAK Figure 17-9 lists a side effect of alcohol that can last well past the 8-hour rule. Which one, and for how long?
options: Impaired night vision and high blood pressure, up to 48 hours
Body dehydration through urine output, up to 24 hours
Inner-ear disturbance and spatial disorientation, up to 48 hours
Drowsiness and dizziness that keep coming back, up to 72 hours
quiz.why: Figure 17-9 lists inner-ear disturbance and spatial disorientation (up to 48 hours) among alcohol's side effects [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]]. Night vision and blood pressure are on the nicotine line, dehydration on the caffeine line, recurring drowsiness on the antihistamine line.

quiz.q: Which SRM grade means the learner needs to be prompted to identify risks and make decisions?
options: Practice
Explain
Manage/Decide
Not Observed
quiz.why: At the Explain level the learner can identify and describe the risks but needs prompting [[25:32|AIH 1-28]].

quiz.q: Your learner starts a go-around and reaches for the mic to tell the tower first. What order does the AIH teach?
options: Power, airspeed and configuration first; tell the tower after those
Tell the tower first so ATC can protect the airspace, then add power
Retract all the flaps at once, then call the tower, then add full power
Call the tower and retrim at the same time, then configure the airplane
quiz.why: During a go-around, adding power, gaining airspeed and properly configuring the airplane come first; informing the tower of the balked landing comes only after these tasks [[25:29|AIH 1-25]].

final_quiz.q: You plan the PHAK's spatial disorientation demonstrations for a learner. Which plan fits the PHAK?
options: Have the learner practice them solo first, so they are relaxed for the dual flight
Fly them in the traffic pattern, so the ground stays close as a reference
Fly them at a safe altitude, with you aboard as the instructor pilot
Skip them if the learner says they already understand the leans
final_quiz.why: The maneuvers should not be tried at low altitudes or without an instructor pilot or safety pilot [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

final_quiz.q: After a long, gentle descending turn in haze, your learner rolls wings level and immediately leans to the left, saying the airplane is banked right. What is happening?
options: Coriolis illusion: a head movement in the long turn set the canal fluid moving on a new axis
The leans: the slow bank was below the canal threshold and leveling feels like a bank the other way
Somatogravic illusion: the speed gained in the descent fooled the otolith organs
Autokinesis: staring at one spot in the haze made the horizon seem to tilt
final_quiz.why: Rotation of 2 degrees per second or less goes undetected, and leveling after it can feel like a bank in the opposite direction, so the pilot leans toward the original turn [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

final_quiz.q: On a night cross-country planned at 7,500 ft, your learner says hypoxia only matters above 12,500 ft. What does the AIM say?
options: Night vision can suffer from 5,000 ft, and it suggests oxygen above 5,000 ft at night
He is right: no hypoxia effect of any kind shows in a healthy pilot below 12,500 ft
Night vision suffers only above 10,000 ft, so oxygen is suggested above 10,000 ft at night
Oxygen is suggested at night only above 14,000 ft, where the crew must use it anyway
final_quiz.why: Night vision deteriorates at a cabin pressure altitude as low as 5,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]], and for optimum protection the AIM encourages supplemental oxygen above 10,000 ft by day and above 5,000 ft at night [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

final_quiz.q: A learner who flies well keeps canceling stall lessons, always in good weather. What does the AIH suggest?
options: Assume a hidden medical problem and refer the learner to an AME before the next lesson
Schedule stalls on every single lesson until the cancellations stop, so the fear wears off by repetition
Ignore it: canceling in good weather is the learner's choice and needs no response
The learner may dread the lesson content; explain the maneuver in more detail and encourage
final_quiz.why: Consistent no-go decisions in good weather may come from apprehension about stalls, landings or solo, and more explanation or encouragement can relieve that stress [[25:28|AIH 1-24]].

final_quiz.q: Under stress in the pattern, a learner laughs inappropriately and is extremely over-cooperative; the next lesson he is deeply depressed. What does the AIH say?
options: These are normal reactions to pattern work and need no action from the instructor
These prove a psychological disorder, so stop training and refer him to an AME
These may be abnormal reactions to stress and call for careful evaluation by you
These are early signs of hypoxia, so put the learner on oxygen next lesson
final_quiz.why: None is absolute, but any of these under stress is reason for careful evaluation [[25:48|AIH 2-15]].

final_quiz.q: You have given 7 hours of flight training since 0700. At 1800 a learner asks for a 1.5-hour lesson. What applies?
options: You may, because time spent in ground training does not count toward the limit
You may not; it would exceed 8 hours of flight training in 24 consecutive hours
You may, as long as the learner already holds a pilot certificate of any kind
You may, as long as you take a 30-minute break before the 1.5-hour lesson
final_quiz.why: A flight instructor may not conduct more than 8 hours of flight training in any 24 consecutive hours [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(a)]]; 7 + 1.5 = 8.5.

final_quiz.q: You will give flight training as PIC in a club airplane. Under 61.23, which medical certificate do you need?
options: At least a third-class medical, unless you operate under BasicMed
At least a second-class medical, since flight instruction is paid work
None at all, because a flight instructor certificate never needs a medical
A first-class medical, since you share the controls with a student pilot
final_quiz.why: 61.23(a)(3)(ii) requires at least a third-class medical when exercising flight instructor privileges as PIC or as a required flightcrew member, except under BasicMed (61.113(i)). No medical is needed only when you are neither PIC nor a required crewmember [[60:205|14 CFR 61.23]].

final_quiz.q: You give a flight review to a 2,000-hour pilot in his own airplane. Everything looks smooth. What does the AIH warn you about?
options: Hyperventilation from test anxiety, which experienced pilots often hide
Airsickness, since he is not used to someone else flying his airplane
Nothing: his experience in this airplane removes the human factors risk
Complacency, which is harder to recognize than fatigue
final_quiz.why: Instructors should be especially alert to complacency in experienced learners, for example a flight review in a familiar aircraft [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner's FRAT for a cross-country scores green, but a line of embedded thunderstorms lies on the route. What is the lesson?
options: A green score means go, so the storms need no further review that day
Thunderstorms only matter on a FRAT when the total score is already red
A low score can still hide one extreme risk that the form did not capture
FRATs are made only for multi-crew operations, so the score is meaningless
final_quiz.why: Numerical FRATs should be used with caution: a low score can still contain an unmitigated extreme risk, such as embedded thunderstorms [[25:188|AIH 10-4]].

final_quiz.q: ATC clears your learner to taxi via Bravo, but she turns onto Alpha, the route she always gets. Which error and which defense?
options: Confirmation bias; have her speed up and clear the taxiway before ATC notices
Expectation bias; ask ATC to clarify the clearance, and stop on the ground if unsure
Impulsivity; have her say the antidote 'Not so fast, think first' and continue
Spatial disorientation; have her trust the heading indicator over what she sees
final_quiz.why: Pilots who routinely get the same clearance may perceive it as expected, not as given [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Clear communication and the option to stop the airplane on the ground are defenses [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

final_quiz.q: On a night cross-country, your learner reports feeling less critical and just wants to accept whatever comes after a 4-hour flight above 5,000 ft. What does the AIH say?
options: Late night, fatigue and long flight above 5,000 ft can make pilots more accepting just as the critical phase nears
This is normal relaxation after a long leg, and a relaxed pilot carries less risk
It means the learner is calm and ready for solo night cross-country flights
It is caused only by the autopilot, so hand-flying the descent will cure it
final_quiz.why: The combination can make pilots less discerning, less decisive and more accepting; the 5P check helps catch it [[25:21|AIH 1-17]].

final_quiz.q: A learner says money and family problems have piled up for months and he cannot cope, but he wants to keep flying. What does the PHAK say?
options: This is acute stress; a short break and an easy lesson will bring his performance back
Some stress keeps a pilot alert, so a busy lesson will sharpen his performance
Stress is not a grounding condition in the regulations, so nothing limits his flying
This is chronic stress; he is not safe to use airman privileges and should see a physician
final_quiz.why: Chronic stress exceeds a person's ability to cope and makes performance fall off rapidly; pilots at this level are not safe, should not exercise their airman privileges and should consult a physician [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner slept 4 hours and says she feels fine at preflight. Per the AIH, when do the fatigue symptoms tend to show?
options: Right at preflight, so feeling fine then means she is rested enough to fly
Only in the flare, when the workload is highest and timing matters most
Once established on altitude and heading, after preflight and departure
Never in flight, because the stress of flying keeps a tired pilot awake
final_quiz.why: Sleep-deprived pilots may not notice sleepiness or other fatigue symptoms during preflight and departure; once underway and established on altitude and heading, the symptoms tend to show [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].

takeaways: You fly with two pilots' aeromedical risks: run IMSAFE on yourself, and build trust so learners tell you about illness and medicine early.
Fatigue and many illnesses show to you before the learner feels them: watch timing errors, skipped secondary tasks and irritability.
Teach the semicircular canal threshold, then demonstrate disorientation at a safe altitude with a briefed exchange of controls.
Optical illusions follow one pattern: feel high, fly low; feel low or close, fly high. Use the altimeter and the glidepath lights.
The alcohol rule is three limits: 8 hours, 0.04, and not under the influence; the AIM's 12 to 24 hours is the smart number.
Teach ADM by scenarios and let the learner decide; grade SRM as Explain, Practice, Manage/Decide.
Name a hazardous attitude or a bias the moment you see it, and teach the antidote or the defense.
cfi_notes: The PHAK's Figure 17-1 lists 30 minutes or more of useful consciousness at 20,000 ft [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], while the AIM says corrective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. Teach the AIM numbers.

The PHAK says nose drops or sprays may reduce the risk of an ear blockage with minor congestion, after checking with an AME [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]]. The AIM says sprays and drops usually do not give adequate protection and the prevention is not flying with an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergy [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Teach the AIM.

The PHAK says hypoxia symptoms vary with the individual [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]; the AIM says they do not vary in an individual [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Both can be true: symptoms differ between people but repeat in one person, which is why chamber training works.

The PHAK states blood alcohol must be less than .04 percent [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]] and the RMH says below 0.04 percent [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]; 14 CFR 91.17 says 0.04 or greater in blood or breath is prohibited and defines the units [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]. Teach the CFR wording.

On workload, the AIH says the first effect is that the pilot begins to work faster [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]; the PHAK says working harder but accomplishing less [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Teach both as the same early warning.

The AIH calls environmental stressors 'physical stress' [[25:28|AIH 1-24]] and the PHAK figure calls them 'environmental' [[1:61|PHAK 2-22]]. Same idea, different label; do not let a learner get stuck on the word.
Hypothermia is on the ACS but in none of the FAA handbooks used here. On the checkride, say so plainly and give what the sources say about cold, then name where you would get the medical facts.

Professional crew pilots who come to you for training in their own airplane may be strong in CRM and threat and error management but new to single-pilot risk management without company support [[25:190|AIH 10-6]].

RMH Figure 2-9 is drawn with one adjustment beside each factor row, which a learner may read as Pilot = ceiling, Aircraft = visibility and so on. The RMH's own worked example (night cross-country to an unfamiliar airport after a full workday adds 1,000 ft ceiling, 1 mile visibility and 1,000 ft runway) applies the adjustments once per factor [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Teach the worked example, and remind learners the figure is only a starting point.
gaps: No source used here defines hypothermia or gives its symptoms, prevention or treatment; get it from a medical or first-aid source or an AME.
The PHAK says not to do disorientation demonstrations at low altitude [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]] but gives no minimum altitude; use your school's SOP and the POH.
The sources give no lesson-length limit for learners; the AIH only says fatigue is the primary consideration [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. Set it by judgment and syllabus.
There is no list of acceptable medications in these sources; the PHAK says the regulations have no specific references to medication usage [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. Ask an AME.
Nutrition guidance stops at regular balanced meals, snacks and high-protein meals [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]] [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]; no source gives how long a missed meal takes to matter.

activities.title: True or false: medicine, alcohol and the rules
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: The regulations list stress among the medical conditions that require grounding.
cards.why: False. Stress is not among them, which is why self-assessment matters [[25:12|AIH 1-8]].

cards.s: 14 CFR contains a specific list of medications pilots may not take.
cards.why: False. The regulations include no specific references to medication usage; 61.53 and 91.17 are the rules that apply [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

cards.s: Two aspirin can contribute to hypoxia and hyperventilation.
Caffeine can dehydrate you through increased urine output.
Herbal supplements and energy boosters cannot cause side effects that matter in flight.
cards.why: False. They can come from substances found in medications and have adverse side effects [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

cards.s: Fatigue, stress or dehydration can make a pilot react badly to a drug he has tolerated before.
91.17 lets the FAA ask for drug test results taken within 4 hours after acting as a crewmember.
Cold reduces blood flow to the hands and feet, a form of stagnant hypoxia.

activities.title: Building risk management through training
activities.intro: Put the AIH's risk management teaching steps in order, first to last, then tap Check.
steps: Ground instruction on risk management before the first flight lesson
Instructor demonstrates a non-numerical FRAT on the first few flights
Learner can conduct a basic risk management analysis by the first solo
Learner analyzes solo flights with occasional coaching and debriefs the instructor
Full risk analysis with a FRAT for every dual and solo cross-country, approved by the instructor

activities.title: A full day on the line
activities.intro: You are a CFI with four lessons booked today. Make each call as the day unfolds.

steps.s: 0630. You slept 5 hours after a late evening. Your first lesson is at 0800.
options: Drink extra coffee and fly as planned
Fly, but let the learner do all the flying
Run IMSAFE on yourself honestly and, if you are not rested, change the lesson to ground school or reschedule
Fly the lesson but skip the preflight briefing to save energy
steps.why: Monitor your own aeromedical risks with IMSAFE [[25:191|AIH 10-7]]; if suffering from acute fatigue, stay on the ground [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. The lesson can move to ground school or be rescheduled [[25:191|AIH 10-7]].

steps.s: 1000. Your second learner has a sinus cold and took an oral decongestant. The lesson is pattern work with many descents.
options: Fly with nose spray as backup
Fly but keep descents steep and short
Do a ground lesson instead
Fly, and use Valsalva if it hurts
steps.why: Do not fly with an upper respiratory infection; sprays usually do not protect and oral decongestants can impair performance [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]] [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

steps.s: 1300. On a first steep turn lesson your third learner goes pale and starts sweating.
options: Continue so the learner gets used to it
Terminate the flight, give fresh air, let the learner fly gently back
Do a stall to distract the learner
Give the learner Dramamine and continue
steps.why: End the flight as soon as early sickness appears; fresh air helps and learners do better on the controls [[25:46|AIH 2-13]]. Dramamine is not for the pilot [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

steps.s: 1600. In the pattern your fourth learner fixates on a frequency problem; altitude drifts and he misses a traffic call.
options: Let it continue so he learns
Tell him to fly the airplane first, then stop, think, slow down and prioritize, and offer to take the radio
Take the controls without saying anything
Have him troubleshoot the radio fully before turning base
steps.why: A minor problem that pulls attention from aircraft control is a classic accident start [[25:17|AIH 1-13]]. Teach stop, think, slow down and prioritize, and delegating tasks [[25:30|AIH 1-26]].

steps.s: 1730. After the last landing, your learner says one ear still hurts and sounds muffled since the descent.
options: Tell him it will clear by itself overnight, so no action is needed
If it does not clear shortly after landing, he should see a physician
Take him up again so a climb and descent can equalize it
Give him a decongestant spray and book tomorrow's pattern lesson
steps.why: An ear block brings severe pain and hearing loss that can last hours to days, and the eardrum can rupture in flight or after landing. If it does not clear shortly after landing, a physician should be consulted [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

activities.title: Work the numbers you will teach
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: A learner took a sedating allergy medicine whose dosing interval is 4 hours. Using the PHAK rule, how many hours after the last dose should she wait to fly?
items.why: Five maximal dosing intervals: 5 x 4 = 20 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

items.q: A 5-hour cross-country in moderate summer heat. Using the PHAK guide, how many pints of water should the pilot drink during the flight?
items.why: One pint per hour in moderate heat stress: 5 x 1 = 5 pints [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

items.q: Baseline day ceiling minimum 2,500 ft. Tomorrow: stressful week (pilot), unfamiliar avionics (aircraft) and a must-meet deadline (external). Using the RMH starting point and one adjustment per factor, what ceiling minimum at least?
items.why: One adjustment per factor, as in the RMH example where two factors add 1,000 ft: 2,500 + 3 x 500 = 4,000 ft [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

items.q: Same pilot, baseline day visibility 4 miles and the same three factors. What visibility minimum at least?
items.why: One adjustment per factor, as in the RMH example where two factors add 1 mile: 4 + 3 x 0.5 = 5.5 miles [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

items.q: Between lessons you take a 20-minute power nap. Using the shortest wake-up time in AIH Figure 1-7, how many minutes after you lie down is the earliest you should resume crew duties?
items.why: 20 minutes of nap + at least 15 minutes after waking (15 to 20 minutes) = 35 minutes [[25:18|AIH 1-14]].
